reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it communicates ordinary Sephora shopping and makeup-saving tips involving shipping, samples, rewards, makeovers, and promotional events. A segment discusses buying qualifying Benefit items, returning unwanted items, and keeping the sample, but the speaker does not recommend that conduct. The products are described as personally purchased, and the end screen promotes ordinary channel and social-media engagement rather than financial participation or a payment-and-data request.

citations.quote: we are filming a Sephora hacks video
you guys can spend $10 and I'm pretty sure for the entire year you guys will get free shipping no matter what.
you guys might as well buy it online because you guys get to have at least four Different samples.
split up your order so then you guys can get like six samples instead of three
they have rewards that come out within 2 minutes, those rewards will be gone

opening.argument: The video repeatedly links obtaining free or unusually valuable products to specific viewer actions. Viewers are told to spend $10 for year-long free shipping, place orders for samples, split orders to multiply samples, and pursue rewards that disappear within minutes. Most concerningly, the speaker describes buying qualifying Benefit items, returning the unwanted purchases, and keeping the promotional sample. That is a concrete acquisition pathway: buy, obtain the incentive, then return the qualifying merchandise. The disclaimer that she is “not advising” it does not remove the fact that the method is presented as an available option. The overall pitch is therefore not merely makeup discussion; it encourages viewers to treat ordinary purchases and returns as a route to obtain products for little or no net cost.

citations.quote: You guys can always do that and return what you don't want but keep the sample.
split up your order so then you guys can get like six samples instead of three
those rewards will be gone
you guys can spend $10 and I'm pretty sure for the entire year you guys will get free shipping no matter what.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling these “shopping tips” does not answer the buy-and-return pathway. The speaker expressly tells viewers they can return what they do not want while keeping the promotional item, and calls it an option despite the disclaimer. Nor does describing samples as store benefits establish that the return-and-retain maneuver is authorized. The repeated emphasis on multiplying samples and rapidly claiming scarce rewards reinforces an acquisition-oriented solicitation.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted conduct is a brief, explicitly discouraged aside, not the video's central promise. The surrounding material concerns ordinary samples and rewards attached to purchases, while the speaker identifies the content as a Sephora hacks video. The evidence does not show that Sephora authorizes retaining an incentive after a return, that viewers are guaranteed a net-free product, or that anyone is asked to send money or data to the speaker.

citations.quote: I'm not advising you guys to do that
we are filming a Sephora hacks video
you guys get to have at least four Different samples

opening.argument: Several warning signs appear together: scarcity, rapid timing, repeated refreshing, and promises of high-value rewards from minimal participation. The speaker says rewards may be gone within two minutes, describes only limited quantities, and instructs viewers to refresh repeatedly during a narrow time window. She also presents a $35 purchase as a way to receive a “huge deluxe sample,” and says a $50 purchase could yield around $100 in samples. These claims frame participation as a time-sensitive opportunity with an unusually favorable payoff. Even if the underlying retailer promotions exist, the presentation encourages viewers to chase the reward before it disappears and to calculate purchases by the promotional value. That combination makes the offer resemble a low-barrier reward solicitation rather than neutral product information.

citations.quote: those rewards will be gone
they'll tell you, they'll release these products between 9 and 5pm
you honestly just have to keep refreshing the page
you might literally get 50 dollars from the samples if you spend 50 dollars

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats urgency as proof of ordinary retailing, but it does not explain the unusually specific timing advice or the claimed near-dollar-for-dollar sample payoff. The speaker presents repeated refreshing as the practical route to scarce rewards and tells viewers to schedule purchases around promotional releases. Those are behavioral instructions designed to drive participation, not merely descriptions of cosmetics.

citations.quote: you honestly just have to keep refreshing the page
make sure you guys buy products on if you're going to on Wednesday or on Friday
you might literally get 50 dollars from the samples if you spend 50 dollars

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Scarcity and timing are consistent with limited retail promotions and do not establish deception. The evidence shows purchases, samples, and rewards, but no guaranteed cash return, withdrawal, investment, or payment to the speaker. The “$50” statement is her valuation of sample products, not proof that viewers receive money. The presentation may be enthusiastic, but enthusiasm does not turn a retailer's promotion into a scam.

opening.argument: Although presented as advice for saving money, the video functions as a direct promotional funnel toward repeated Sephora participation. It urges viewers to buy online, split orders, attend events, use codes, claim rewards at precise times, check promotional emails, and purchase on selected days. The title itself advertises “10 Ways to get FREE MAKEUP,” while the conclusion targets viewers who want to “get a bang for your buck.” This framing turns ordinary commerce into an enticing promise of free products and repeatedly directs viewers toward actions that generate purchases or engagement. The channel's visible end screen also invites subscriptions and directs viewers to another video, extending the promotional pathway beyond the shopping tips. The educational framing therefore understates how strongly the content steers viewers toward participation.

citations.quote: SEPHORA HACK: 10 Ways to get FREE MAKEUP?!
you guys might as well buy it online because you guys get to have at least four Different samples.
make sure you guys buy products on if you're going to on Wednesday or on Friday
just wanted some tips on how to get a bang for your buck

rebuttal.rebuttal: The “ordinary tips” characterization overlooks the cumulative calls to action: buy online, split orders, attend events, refresh during release windows, check emails, and purchase on particular days. The title does not merely identify makeup; it promises free makeup through hacks. The visible subscription and social links further show an audience-acquisition component alongside the shopping funnel, rather than a detached review.

citations.quote: 10 Ways to get FREE MAKEUP?!
split up your order so then you guys can get like six samples instead of three
you honestly just have to keep refreshing the page
don't forget to like comment and subscribe

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promotion and instruction are not inherently scams. The title's “free makeup” wording is immediately qualified by shopping actions such as purchases, shipping enrollment, or reward redemption. The end-screen subscription request is ordinary channel engagement, and the description says the products were purchased personally. Nothing cited establishes a hidden fee, false identity, guaranteed monetary return, or a request to transfer funds to the creator.
